query_title: Audit and evaluate apiserver client usage in kubelet
query_body:
The current apiserver client QPS for kubelet is the default 5.0, which is not high for kubelet. When batch creating pods, the startup latency is completely dominated by the QPS (e.g. see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14554#issuecomment-143829191, events consumed most of the bandwidth). Moreover, the _perceived_ kubelet performance may be affected by slight change in kubelet's behavior, due to the QPS limitation (e.g., https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/14554#issuecomment-143898216).

We should audit our apiserver client usage and re-evaluate whether to bump the QPS, or to clearly surface any increase in the client usage.

Major consumers for the apiserver client includes:
- events
- pod status
- node status (relatively low)

The breakdown of starting a pod of N containers (when there is no failure):
- (N+1) \* 3 events (for each container, including the infra container, there are pulled, created, and started events)
- 3 pod status update (the initial pending, running, and finally the running+ready status). This may increase once we let user control per-container probing period.

For starting 30 single-container pods on kubelet, the pods along would generate ((1+1)*3+3)*30= 9*30=270 requests.
This would take kubelet 270/5 qps = 54 seconds to send out.

/cc @kubernetes/goog-node

target_title: Issue with livenessProbe
target_body:
Hi, i spot weird issue with livenessProbe. You can see pod description here https://gist.github.com/roman-shuhov/d5d6c230bb3b86b639be .

I tried to create this pod and it kept restarting, and kubectl describe showed the following error:

`
Liveness probe failed: Get http://website-example-a:80/watcher.html: dial tcp: lookup website-example-a: no such host
`

So, looks like if "host" value is specified in livenessProbe (as in the example above), kubernetes is trying to fetch url http://<host>/<path> instead of sending host as a HTTP header. 

You can actually see this logic in the source code - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/prober.go#L205

The problem is that in this case this request go to the random pod (because it goes through load balancer), so if kubernetes have a bad pod it may kill a healthy one instead.

I think this logic should be changed, because i don't see any reason to make http://<host>/<path> request for the livenessProbe.

target_title: Consistently support graceful and immediate termination for all objects
target_body:
Issue discussed in #103, #1325, #1445, and other issues/PRs.

Our API isn't consistent on clean/graceful shutdown vs. immediate termination of our objects. We should support both modes, and in a consistent fashion. One mode should be the default, and the other should be available via a URL parameter on DELETE or custom verb (e.g., [INLINE_CODE], for graceful shutdown). Graceful shutdown should accept a timeout (as discussed in lifecycle hook PRs) and reason (#1462) as parameters.

Cleanly turning down a replication controller currently requires external orchestration: resizing it to 0 and waiting for pods to be deleted prior to deleting the replication controller itself. 

On the other hand, by default, individual pods are supposed to gracefully terminate, executing their PreStop handlers, SIGTERM handlers, and, in the future, PostStop handlers.

We should define what clean shutdown would mean for a service (wait for all targeted pods to be deleted?).

However, there are definitely occasions when one would not want graceful shutdown (e.g., shutting down a test deployment), and we should support that.

query_title: kube-dns should be the only Nameserver for Pod with DnsPolicy=ClusterFirst
query_body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/15303#issuecomment-146840698

With more than one NS on cluster-first pods, the problems are: 
1. Faulty NXDomain Problem:
 If skydns were to fail, clients on a pod (with clusterDnsPolicy) will start getting NXDOMAIN for *cluster.local lookups instead of SERVFAIL(which could have signaled clients to retry), from the second NS
2. Faulty Resolution Problem:
 If skydns were to fail, clients on a pod (with clusterFirst DnsPolicy) might accidentally get the wrong IP.
 Consider that a k8s user has created a service called "mail".
 Assume that the search paths are "default.svc.cluster.local google.com"
 Ideally, the Query should be resolved by skydns for mail.default.svc.cluster.local.
 But since Skydns is down, the Query gets resolved by the fallback nameserver for mail.google.com

The Faulty Resolution Problem exists even if skydns is used in no-rec mode.
- We need to exercise caution while doing this because skydns needs to be robust enough.
 Otherwise ClusterFirst containers will be badly impacted with skydns being their only NS. 
 (skydns will be in recurse mode)
- We should have atleast 2 instances of kube-dns running for High Availability.
 (And also because kubelet has a backoff policy if any pod restarts too many times in a certain time window)
- SkyDNS will use the other NS for queries that don't end in ".cluster.local" (domain param of skydns)

target_body:
Right now, our label selectors support conjunctions of exact matches of key-value pairs. We should support conjunctions of:
- key exists

query_title: HPA controller needs more flexibility from APIInstaller
query_body:
Spawned from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177

 Our [INLINE_CODE] infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the [INLINE_CODE] client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale.

// pulling a few comments from the original issue
1. HPA is a central component that should be able to reach out to generic endpoints
2. HPA can only know about a limited number of versions and conversions internally (anything compiled with kube)
3. We want HPA to be able to scale anything that results in pods generically, by virtue of invoking a generic Scale sub resource on endpoints
4. HPA will therefore have to be able to submit things it knows about to endpoints it does not know about.
5. Therefore an API server has to be able to accept the things HPA knows about (Scale, Kube group, v1) and convert it internally to its own recognized format (Scale, OpenShift/3rd party group, v2).
6. Therefore we need to relax the APIInstaller limitation and allow clients to convert.
 @bgrant0607 @lavalamp i think this walks back the previous decision we had to not accept multiple types of input - there is no way for HPA to scale things it doesn't know about unless it can send things to a remote server that it knows about. The remote server is responsibility for taking the Kube type submitted by HPA and converting it to its own internal format.

The contract between HPA controller client and remote API groups that implement Scale is "I will send you one of a set of API versions that I recognize".

@kubernetes/goog-csi @DirectXMan12 @ncdc @smarterclayton
target_title: HPA needs to handle discovery, controller credentials, privilege escalation protection
target_body:
When integrating the HPA controller, we've hit a couple issues.
1. The HPA controller takes an APIGroup, APIVersion, Kind (this should probably have been resource) and attempts to call a [INLINE_CODE] operation on it. Right now, that's based on a client building a URL. That client needs to be able to perform API discovery operations in order to locate where the particular (group, version, resource) tuple lives. Right now it doesn't.
2. This intersects with authorization because the HPA controller needs to have valid credentials for every (group, version, resource) tuple that it can manipulate. Given that the end goal is to have some APIGroups hosted in different locations (consider kube and openshift not living in the same API server), we need to have a way to initialize the HPA controller with correct credentials.
3. Because the HPA controller may escalate the user's authority to actually perform the scale operation, the HPA REST endpoint should perform some authorization of the HPA resource when it is created. One option is to do this via the [INLINE_CODE] mechanism described here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12209. The remote API is probably needed because you'd want to authorize based on the authorization engine of the API server hosting the (grouip, version, resource). In the short term, even accepting an [INLINE_CODE] would get you part way.
4. Our APIInstaller infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the HPAController client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177#issuecomment-1518316

target_title: Possible future improvements for Job object
target_body:
1. (COMPLETE) set a deadline and kill the job after that deadline . This was called ActiveDeadlineSeconds in the original proposal. I argued for removing it for now and it was dropped during review. @bgrant0607 argues that we have tried (on Borg) offering users many options for managing/throttling failures, and none of them worked well for users except deadlines for non-serving jobs. 
2. automatically throttle creation of new pods when failures are frequent.
3. distinguish between "application failures" and "cluster failures" (e.g. machine-level OOM, node failure) in reporting failures, and in throttling. 
4. consider interaction of Pods of a Job with Vertical Autoscaler. That is, I should be able to start a job with an initial prediction of memory usage, and then if it OOMs, modify the request and retry. 
5. ensure that successful pods are not automatically deleted before the Job finishes (because then the Job Manager will forget about the success). Either mark the pod as do-not-garbage-collect, or else record the success somewhere else.
6. Show relevant pod events in Job describe output.
7. Ensure graceful deletion works when reducing parallelism
8. Indexed Job feature: when each Pod is created, manager decides which "completion index" it is trying to do. Ensures one completion for each index from 0 to [INLINE_CODE]. target_title: Expose secrets to containers in environment variables
target_body:
Now that #4126 and #4514 have landed, it should be possible to expose secrets to containers as environment variables. While this is arguably not the optimal way to consume secrets, it will be important to users taking their first steps into a cloud environment, and we should offer this feature to enable a good experience for users who need it. For what it's worth, we consider this to be an important use-case for users of [OpenShift](https://github.com/openshift/origin).

Let's start with getting all the requirements and challenges on the table:
1. How should this be modeled in the API?

We found the scheduler component is the bottleneck of starting pods. And it spents most of the time in an external pkg (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L27) that handling math operations.

## Objective

The purpose of this document is to consolidated the major Kubernetes Volume issues/feature requests, and introduce high-level designs that ensure alignment between all of them.
## Background

There are three big designs currently being considered for Kubernetes Volume Storage:
1. Dynamic Provisioning of Volumes

target_title: HPA controller needs more flexibility from APIInstaller
target_body:
Spawned from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177

 Our [INLINE_CODE] infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the [INLINE_CODE] client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale.

// pulling a few comments from the original issue
1. HPA is a central component that should be able to reach out to generic endpoints
2. HPA can only know about a limited number of versions and conversions internally (anything compiled with kube)
3. We want HPA to be able to scale anything that results in pods generically, by virtue of invoking a generic Scale sub resource on endpoints
4. HPA will therefore have to be able to submit things it knows about to endpoints it does not know about.
5. Therefore an API server has to be able to accept the things HPA knows about (Scale, Kube group, v1) and convert it internally to its own recognized format (Scale, OpenShift/3rd party group, v2).
6. Therefore we need to relax the APIInstaller limitation and allow clients to convert.
 @bgrant0607 @lavalamp i think this walks back the previous decision we had to not accept multiple types of input - there is no way for HPA to scale things it doesn't know about unless it can send things to a remote server that it knows about. The remote server is responsibility for taking the Kube type submitted by HPA and converting it to its own internal format.

The contract between HPA controller client and remote API groups that implement Scale is "I will send you one of a set of API versions that I recognize".

query_body:
Add something like
[INLINE_CODE] to [INLINE_CODE]

Semantics is: if the pod is managed by a replication controller, scheduler will try to put the replacement pod on a node different from the one where the pod you are deleting was previously running. (If the pod is not managed by a replication controller, then the option has no effect.)

Proposed implementation is
- add [INLINE_CODE] field to [INLINE_CODE]
- before deleting the pod, API server (registry, I think) adds an annotation to the pod (maybe key [INLINE_CODE] and no value)
- modify the controllers so that when they see this annotation added to a pod, they cache the name of the pod P and the name of the node N it is running on; when they see the deletion and go to create the replacement pod for P, they add a SoftNodeAffinity for "node name is not N" (I just realized this feature is dependent on implementation of #18261 since we can't express this today, and also dependent on exposing node name as a node label which is part of #9044)

This should work even if the controller fails between the update and the deletion, but not if the controller fails between the deletion and creating the replacement pod. This should be OK as the feature is "best effort" (we intentionally use SoftNodeAffinity instead of HardNodeAffinity).

This is a pre-requisite for rescheduler, so it can create a hole for a pending pod to schedule into, without having the pod that was previously in that hole schedule back into the space first.

However there are other uses, for example a human operator might want to move a pod off a node for some reason (maybe it is receiving or producing interference from/to another pod on that node).

This was originally discussed in this comment
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/12140#issuecomment-15
target_title: Create a rescheduler
target_body:
It's premature to start working on this, but I wanted to jot down some notes collected from past conversations and experience on this topic (and I noticed we didn't have an issue for this yet).

A rescheduler is an agent that proactively causes currently-running Pods to be moved, so as to optimize some objective function for goodness of the layout of Pods in the cluster. (The objective function doesn't have to be expressed mathematically; it may just be a collection of ad-hoc rules, but in principle there is an objective function. Implicitly an objective function is described by the scheduler's predicate and priority functions.) It might be triggered to run every N minutes, or whenever some event happens that is known to make the objective function worse (for example, whenever a Pod goes PENDING for a long time.)

A rescheduler is useful because without a rescheduler, scheduling decisions are only made at the time Pods are created. But as the cluster layout changes over time, free "holes" are often produced that were not available when a Pod was initially scheduled. These holes are produced by run-to-completion Pods terminating, empty nodes being added by a node auto-scaler, etc. Moving already-running Pods into these holes may lead to a better cluster layout. A rescheduler might not just exploit existing holes, but also create holes by evicting Pods (assuming it knows they can reschedule elsewhere), as in free space defragmentation. 

[Although alluded to above, it's worth emphasizing that rescheduling is the only way to make use of new nodes added by a cluster auto-scaler (unless Pods were already PENDING; but even then, it's likely advantageous to put more than just the previously PENDING Pods on the new nodes.)]

query_title: Next Step for Private Registry addon
query_body:
Continuing discussion in #1319 
## Current state:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/cluster/addons/registry
## What can be done:
1. Switch the kube-registry image storage to use GCS/S3.
2. Expose external ip for kube-registry. Better with TLS and authentication enabled. 
3. On each node, add kube-registry as insecure-registry. This can be done by setting flag KUBE_ENABLE_INSECURE_REGISTRY=true when running kube-up.sh. With this setup, there is no need to have registry proxy on each node. Kubelet can pull image using registry service ip. It would be nice if we could use the DNS name of kube-registry service. But kube-dns currently does not work on node.
4. Enable authentication with htpass. htpass file can be packed into a secret. 
5. Enable TLS with certificate signed by cluster CA or provided by user. Cert can be packed into a secret. 
## Open Questions:
1. How to get a resolvable name for kube-registry on each node? Maybe we can add an entry in /etc/hosts for now?
2. I tried to set up a registry with self-signed cert. If the cert uses registry ip as common name, then I will get the exact same problem described here:
 https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/8943
 http://stackoverflow.com/questions/23468530/use-docker-registry-with-ssl-certifictae-without-ip-sans
 It looks like the registry only works with certificates using domain names as CN. This comes back to question #1
3. What is the ideal way to interact with kube-registry from outside of the k8s cluster? Proxy? Port-forwarding? External IP? With SSL or insecure? 
4. What should be the out-of-the-box features?

query_title: [User Story] Improve HPA to bring to GA
query_body: - [x] HPA needs to handle discovery, controller credentials, privilege escalation protection - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177
target_title: HPA needs to handle discovery, controller credentials, privilege escalation protection
target_body:
When integrating the HPA controller, we've hit a couple issues.
1. The HPA controller takes an APIGroup, APIVersion, Kind (this should probably have been resource) and attempts to call a [INLINE_CODE] operation on it. Right now, that's based on a client building a URL. That client needs to be able to perform API discovery operations in order to locate where the particular (group, version, resource) tuple lives. Right now it doesn't.
2. This intersects with authorization because the HPA controller needs to have valid credentials for every (group, version, resource) tuple that it can manipulate. Given that the end goal is to have some APIGroups hosted in different locations (consider kube and openshift not living in the same API server), we need to have a way to initialize the HPA controller with correct credentials.
3. Because the HPA controller may escalate the user's authority to actually perform the scale operation, the HPA REST endpoint should perform some authorization of the HPA resource when it is created. One option is to do this via the [INLINE_CODE] mechanism described here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/12209. The remote API is probably needed because you'd want to authorize based on the authorization engine of the API server hosting the (grouip, version, resource). In the short term, even accepting an [INLINE_CODE] would get you part way.
4. Our APIInstaller infrastructure forces all requests for a particular version of a REST endpoint to use an exactly matching version (POSTs to api/v1/namespace/foo/resource must send a v1 object). This breaks the HPAController client because it cannot generically include every codec for every (group, kind) that it might want to scale. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/16177#issuecomment-1518316

query_title: [User Story] Secrets should be exposed to containers as environment variables
query_body: - [x] Expose secrets to containers in environment variables - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4710
target_title: Expose secrets to containers in environment variables
target_body:
Now that #4126 and #4514 have landed, it should be possible to expose secrets to containers as environment variables. While this is arguably not the optimal way to consume secrets, it will be important to users taking their first steps into a cloud environment, and we should offer this feature to enable a good experience for users who need it. For what it's worth, we consider this to be an important use-case for users of [OpenShift](https://github.com/openshift/origin).

Let's start with getting all the requirements and challenges on the table:
1. How should this be modeled in the API?
2. What limits are reasonable to place on secrets exposed to containers this way? For example, there are different upper limits on aspects of environment variables on different platforms.
3. Secrets are not static but environment variables are. Should the consuming containers be restarted when a secret value changes?
4. Should environment variables containing secrets be exposed via [INLINE_CODE]*?
5. Environment variables that contain secrets should not be captured by [INLINE_CODE]*

*Applies to future equivalencies in other supported container runtimes

On all aspects of the problem mentioned above, we should take into account possible cross-cuts with:
1. Pass pod info to container (#560)
2. Dynamic configuration (#1553)
3. Sundry other things collected under the downward/upward API aggregator (#386)

query_title: Moving kube-proxy out of kube node
query_body:
Current Kubernetes Deployment Mode is putting Kubelet and Kubeproxy together in the same kube node, I tried to move the kube-proxy out of the node and put it into the Service gateway node which doesn't have Pod on that. 
![kube diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cheyang/kubernetes_cd/master/kube.jpg)
The configuration in Node is like this:

[CODE_BLOCK]

This can work. Here are my thoughts of this deployment mode.

**Advantage**:
1. Make the compute resource in kube node only for Pods. As we know the kube-proxy will consume a lot of CPUs, Memories, IOs and Networks resources especially when using userland proxy in heavy load.
2. Service Gateway node can be focused as a route device, and even no need for route capability for kube-proxy. We can only depend on route and iptables kernel level capabilities. 
3. No changes in existing iptables rule in Kube node.There are some default iptables rules conflicting and overwritten in kube nodes, so simplifying the iptables configuration in kube nodes are good for App Operators. See [issue 10692](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/10692)

**Disadvantage:**
1. The Service gateway is the single failure point
2. The Service gateway node has to be the in the same Layer 2 network with kube nodes which should be routed by it.

I am planning to use this deployment in our product env. I want to get the comments from kubernetes experts about this. 

Can you let me know the advantages and disadvantages in your perspectives. Thanks.

target_title: Standalone cAdvisor for monitoring
target_body:
As of Kubernetes v1.1, and possibly v1.2 as well, cAdvisor is linked into kubelet.
Kubelet groups detailed cAdvisor metrics into pods and nodes and exposes them via REST endpoints ([INLINE_CODE])

Monitoring is resource intensive. There are currently several issues filed against kubelet around resource usage which are mostly related to cAdvisor's resource consumption.
Support for custom metrics adds significant resource overhead to kubelet.

Not all users of kubernetes need cAdvisor for monitoring.

Kubelet will need just a few metrics for its functionality. Specifically, cpu usage, memory usage, and filesystem usage for now. These metrics are needed for scheduling and other cluster functionalities.

By separating out cAdvisor monitoring agent from kubelet, users can choose to run cAdvisor as a standalone container and get a lot more detailed metrics. 
This split will let us optimize resource impact of kubelet and cadvisor independently.
cAdvisor can expose potentially expensive metrics as well.

For the basic metrics that kubelet needs, it will embed specific libraries from cAdvisor and compute those metrics internally.

cAdvisor needs to be enhanced to support pods. To make this easier, kubelet should expose the pods that it is currently managing via some API. (#9473 talks about one such API)

query_title: Nodecontroller reassigns CIDR of first node on restart
query_body:
If the node controller ever restarts (like we do periodically in the daemon restart test, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19023) it will reassign the CIDR of the first node. This can cause all sorts of problems like docker and container restart, pod phase changing etc. 

This code seems to be at fault:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/node/nodecontroller.go#L545

I feel like I'm missing some context here, which is why I haven't uploaded a pr. 
We don't generate available cidrs before checking that the first node is in the set (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/node/nodecontroller.go#L550). But then break out of the loop to generate cidrs a little later, saving the other nodes (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/node/nodecontroller.go#L568). 

Do we only need to generate available cidrs once on startup? that sounds like the sensible thing unless there's a GKE subnet requirement I'm missing.

query_title: Kubeproxy should always apply latest snapshot
query_body:
This bug is mostly to document the flow that most likely leads to the latency observed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/20402.
1. Watch comes in, sends an update/add/del to proxiers api source: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/config/api.go#L56
2. ApiSource snapshots all services or endpoints and shoves them in a channel: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/client/cache/undelta_store.go#L57
3. Merger pulls out of this channel, inserts into shared map, and sends notification down the update channel: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/config/config.go#L156
4. Proxy notices update, invokes [INLINE_CODE]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/proxy/config/config.go#L276

If running OnEndpointsUpdate takes 100ms during which 4 other endpoints come down the watch, we'll perform 1-4 for each. Instead, if the update channel in step 3 is full we can just go back to pulling out new watch snapshots from 1. This will drop intermediate updates.

query_title: Kubelet: We should define Container Waiting state better.
query_body:
In Kubernetes, there are 3 [INLINE_CODE]: [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE]. Among them, [INLINE_CODE] is pretty straight forward, but [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] are a bit ambiguous, especially [INLINE_CODE]. Even in the [official document](http://kubernetes.io/v1.1/docs/user-guide/pod-states.html), there is no specific definition for these 3 states.

For user, they need to know what these states mean, so they could inspect the system better.
For developer, the ambiguity really makes the [code](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L3239) messy and buggy. 

In the current implementation, container will be considered to be [INLINE_CODE] in 3 situations:
- The container is to be started for the first time but hasn't been started yet.
- The container is in backoff crash loop.
- All historic containers are garbage collected, the container is treated as a newly started one. (This is a bug, not what we really expect)

Is this exactly what [INLINE_CODE] means? If so, we should document it and cleanup the code. If not, we should define it.

There are some possible definitions:
1) Only before container is successfully started **for the first time**, it is [INLINE_CODE].
The lifecycle of a container should be:

[CODE_BLOCK]

2) **Each time**, after container is tried to be restarted in [INLINE_CODE] but before it is observed by [INLINE_CODE], it is [INLINE_CODE]. 
The lifecycle of a container should be:

[CODE_BLOCK]

3) Only if the container will never be restarted again, it is [INLINE_CODE], otherwise it is [INLINE_CODE].
The lifecycle of a container should be:

[CODE_BLOCK]

I think option 2) should be better.

target_title: Improve e2e test coverage of services
target_body:
What's currently included in the services e2e test:
https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/service.go
1. Services should serve a basic endpoint from pods
2. Services should serve multiport endpoints from pods
3. Services should be able to create a functioning external load balancer
4. Services should be able to create a functioning NodePort service
5. Services should be able to change the type and nodeport settings of a service
6. Services should release the load balancer when Type goes from LoadBalancer -> NodePort
7. Services should prevent NodePort collisions
8. Services should check NodePort out-of-range
9. Services should release NodePorts on delete
10. Services should correctly serve identically named services in different namespaces on different external IP addresses

What's not yet covered (and there are surely more than what's in the following list):

target_title: Don't use ":latest" or non-tagged images in e2e tests
target_body:
If a image is not tagged or is tagged with :latest, the image pull policy is defaulted to PullAlways. This causes unnecessary image pulling in e2e tests, leading to various timeout flakes (e.g. #20418).

target_title: AWS: We should add a rate limiter to AWS API calls
target_body:
We had a few bugs where we would get into loops which would cause us to get into fast-retries loop, and often we would exhaust AWS API quota. Sometimes this would even cause AWS to send a warning email. e.g. #11979 

@brendandburns suggested in https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/issues/11979#issuecomment-126502901 that:

> We should probably add a rate limiter into the AWS client, like we did for GCE:
> https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/util/throttle.go

That seems like something we should have; we should obviously fix any bugs which cause fast-retry loops, but we should have a second layer-of-defense as well. Also if someone launches a thousand services which require an ELB each, we want to respect the AWS API rate limits, even if we don't have a bug per-se.

query_title: LoadBalancer creation retry happens every second
query_body:
From customer logs, it looks like we retry to create a LoadBalancer after a failure every second. This causes rate-limiting problems on AWS (and probably will on GCE also?). We should have a less aggressive retry policy.

Related #21625
target_title: The servicecontroller loop is racy
target_body:
In pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go, we start 10 goroutines that process service events: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L139-L141

Each of these workers then locks on a per-service mutex when processing events: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/service/servicecontroller.go#L225-L228

But I believe there is no guarantee that the order of lock acquisition is the same as the order of events. Thus I think we might process events out of order when services change rapidly.

An alternative design might be to have a per-service goroutine with a per-service event queue. This would mean that service events would be guaranteed to be processed in order. It would also make caching of the previous state much simpler. Finally, when we hit an error like a failure to create a LoadBalancer, we could simply sleep without risking exhausting our "thread pool".

make keys secret KEY=/tmp/nginx.key CERT=/tmp/nginx.crt SECRET=/tmp/secret.json

Recommend:

Add documentation that explicitly documents (separately) how to generate a Kubernetes secret from self-signed certificates.

Please add (if there's not already) an easier way to submit bugs against kubernetes.io by he

target_title: Kubernetes on AWS should be Multi-AZ by default
target_body:
Hello!

 I thought I'd open an issue, as I am currently working on this and hope to have a commit ready by the end of the day.

 "kube-up" with AWS ought to build out a highly available and multi-AZ kubernetes cluster following AWS EC2 best practices. There are two large steps to this:
1. Multi-AZ minions
2. Highly available / Multi-AZ master

I am only focusing on goal #1 here. These changes center entirely in cluster/aws/util.sh. However, I will need to modify the actual provider code in Go because, while AWS ELBs are brought up with the proper subnets, it appears they do not have multi-availability zone routing enabled.

 I am leaving the security groups in place and creating a secondary subnet and secondary autoscaling group. NUM_MINIONS is now split into NUM_MINIONS_PRIMARY_ZONE and NUM_MINIONS_SECONDARY_ZONE. query_title: Admission controllers can cause unnecessary significant load on apiserver
query_body:
Recently we observed high latencies on POST pods on our scalability tests.
For more context see: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/22340

It appeared to be throttling related, e.g.:

[CODE_BLOCK]

As an example look at resource quota admission controller.
In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/20446 there was some fallback added to use lru cache in case of on objects.
However, not what happens if we are sending multiple POST pods at the same time to apiserver.
What happens in Admit() if there are no results in Indexer, we list ResourceQuotas.
But if there are multiple calls at the same time, there can be multiple LISTs before the cache is updated:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/resourcequota/admission.go#L131
But this can cause throttling of these requests.

What we should do is: if there is List() in flight, we should wait until it is finished and lookupCache is updated.

### Edit: a lot has change since this original issue description, read the later comments

It's time to declare bankruptcy on [INLINE_CODE]. It served us dutifully but has grown to be unmaintainable. Let's learn form our experience and start building v2.

Some possible improvements I would like to see:
- use ansible, the technology the community settled on
 - or, ideally, eliminate all of Chef/Puppet/Ansible/Salt
 - concrete problems include:
 - Salt and/or python can't be installed on some distros and consumes a lot of space: # 27547
 - People already using one of C/P/A/S don't want to use 2 different systems on the same nodes

- as little as possible should be installed on hosts
- (eventually) reduce configuration bits by implementing kubelet bootstrap #23172
- kubelet (and maybe the underlying container runtime) should be the only init unit that we install
- use systemd in place of supervisord
- fewer configuration options, fewer differences for different environments
- kubelet is the only thing on the host but will eventually run in a container as well.
 - deploy kube-proxy and fluentd in daemonsets as addons
- installation artifact, which is separate from release artifact, should only package kubelet (until kubelet is run in a container) and various ansible config files. everything else should be pulled from an external docker registry.

This is more of an open question, should we teach the Ingress about TCP?

If we fold TCP into Ingress:
- Everything in the Ingress is about entry into the cluster 
- Everything in the Service is intra cluster (ips, algorithms, affinity etc) 
- Type=NodePort will continue to be an escape hatch for Services

This would enable us to leverage the Ingress for things like SSL routing (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19333), and leverage Service.Type=Loadbalancer for internal lb (whatever form that takes). 

**How to express type=loadbalancer?**

Create an Ingress like:

[CODE_BLOCK]

kubectl expose would do this (discussion on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/17429 needs to converge). 

**How to express SNI?**

[CODE_BLOCK]

If the above spec is defined _with_ a TLS section, the Ingress controller will terminate the connection using SNI to figure out which certs to serve. Discussion on: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/19333

**Do we need to express TCP frontend ports?**

The challenge here is defining a frontend port that we don't really need for HTTP (:80 and :443 are implicit). One way is:

[CODE_BLOCK]

Another option is to disallow [INLINE_CODE], the Ingress controller just picks one and writes it to Status (on GCE a port is not needed). All that matters is that TCP traffic reaches the backend. For legacy apps that _need_ a port, they create multiple ingresses with a [INLINE_CODE] annotation that the Ingress controller tries to honor.

query_title: API: use cases for kubectl attach?
query_body:
In the rkt container engine integration we are trying to get full feature parity with the existing k8s API. We are very close.

The most recent snag we hit though is that rkt does not support the concept of "attach". For those who aren't familiar see the help output of [INLINE_CODE]:

[CODE_BLOCK]

The reason rkt doesn't support this is quite practical: for applications that are long running we attach the applications stdout/stdin to a logging daemon without a man-in-the-middle. And the stdin is attached to stdin because this is sort of the accepted default for most long-running processes.

Now, rkt does support interactive applications with [INLINE_CODE]. But, you chose to do interactive ahead of time which means we skip attaching stdout/stdin/stderr to the log daemon and attach it to the calling process instead.

So, attach is this weird middle ground between [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] which is rather odd. I really don't understand the use case and the k8s issue introducing attach isn't super helpful either: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/1521

I want to understand what are the use cases for attach and if we can do one of the following things:

1) Simply not support it in the rkt integration because the use cases are so narrow and the complexity is high to implement it

2) Remove attach from the next revision of the API, I feel like nearly all use cases of debugging can be handled with exec or even a proper session inside of the container created with sshd, etc.

3) Enumerate the compelling use cases for attach so we have some concrete use cases to justify the complexity of figuring this out inside of rkt

rkt upstream issue: https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/1799
target_title: Support attach
target_body:
Forked from #1503.

We should decide whether we will support [Docker attach to stdin and stdout](https://docs.docker.com/reference/api/docker_remote_api_v1.13/#attach-to-a-container). It would be convenient for interactive containers and, more importantly, short-running, run-once data-in/data-out containers, such as for configuration generators, workflow steps, cron jobs, etc.

Support would likely be similar to that required to support run in container (aka docker exec) and/or ssh (#1513).

/cc @vishh

target_title: Strategy for pods sharing same host port ?
target_body:
I don't know if kubernetes is currently supporting or has plans to provide a capability for two or more pods to be sharing the same port on the node with same public ip address. Same way like nginx and apache can host multiple websites on the same ip by named based virtual hosting. 

Lets say I have 2 pods and each pod hosts a wordpress app on port 80. It could be expensive to provide a public ip for each pod, plus I don't know if kubernetes even supports multiple public ips. 

I was wondering what are options for accomplishing something like that with kubernetes. 

One way I was thinking is by running an Nginx or other proxy service one each node, which would proxy requests based on the domain name to internal pod IPs. 
Maybe kubernetes could expand it's current proxy system to offer this capability as well ?

Are there any other ways as well ?

query_title: Cluster addon resource usage needs to be tracked and tested
query_body:
We're seeing some failures for customers that upgrade to k8s 1.2 because the various addons now require more cluster node resources to run (i.e. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23556). Customers with high cluster utilization or small machine/node configuration may have situations where their v1.1 cluster no longer works properly after an upgrade to 1.2 because of this.

At the least, we need to track the resource utilization/reservation of addons, with a test that also fails if this increases (i.e. a test that schedules an "almost all free resource" pod that fails if kube-system pods resource use increases). Any increase needs to be investigated and justified (it is a "breaking change" of sorts, since it may result in a non-working clusters for some customers). 

Related issues: 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13695
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13048
target_title: Feature request: dynamic cluster addon resizer
target_body:
People create clusters at a wide range of sizes. People then resize clusters to a wide range of sizes. Our cluster addons are configured statically, and do not respond to such changes in size. This causes problems in some cases:
1. The default addons don't all fit on sufficiently small clusters (e.g. create a cluster with a single f1-micro on GCE, prepare to feel the pain) 
2. The default addons waste a large proportion of resources on small clusters -- does my two node cluster 300MiB for heapster? Will it ever need more than one DNS pod?
3. The default addons don't scale properly to large clusters - heapster with 300MiB of memory isn't going to cut it on even some medium sized clusters, let alone clusters with a hundred nodes ([example](https://groups.google.com/d/topic/google-containers/LlXw0xJqWMI/discussion)). More than one DNS pod will be useful for availability.

Some really simple control logic should be able to make the situation better by listing the nodes in the cluster and updating the addon RCs using a few basic rules. It could be part of the node controller, or be a very small container that runs on the master or even in the user's cluster (but it better be very small to justify its benefits).

@roberthbailey @zmerlynn

query_title: Kubelet: Kubelet built with go(<= 1.4) won't work with docker built with go(>=1.6)
query_body:
After #23506, Kubelet built with go(<= 1.4) won't work with docker built with go(>=1.6).

@andyzheng0831 reported that #23506 broke our Jenkins trusty built https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23506#issuecomment-204757239. Thank @eparis for pointing me to https://github.com/docker/docker/issues/20865.

After some digging, I found out why this happened:
1. After https://github.com/golang/go/commit/6e11f45ebdbc7b0ee1367c80ea0a0c0ec52d6db5, the http server in Go 1.6 will validate the [HTTP Host header](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.23) conforming to HTTP 1.1 (See https://github.com/golang/go/issues/13624)
2. On the http client side, Go writes the HTTP Host header with [INLINE_CODE] or [INLINE_CODE](if the former is empty) (See [here](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/a6557a05a03490af3b26f97f9a4ce99c7c773fe5/src/net/http/request.go#L404-L410))
3. When using the [default docker endpoint](https://github.com/docker/engine-api/blob/68a7b6bebf8f57d559b7788a46c55045438747b9/client/client_unix.go#L6) ([INLINE_CODE]), engine-api will set [INLINE_CODE], [INLINE_CODE] (See [set request.URL.Host](https://github.com/docker/engine-api/blob/68a7b6bebf8f57d559b7788a46c55045438747b9/client/request.go#L85-L87) and [set request.Host](https://github.com/docker/engine-api/blob/68a7b6bebf8f57d559b7788a46c55045438747b9/client/request.go#L131))
4. When the engine-api is built with Go >= 1.5, everything goes well, because Go will [clean up the Host](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/net/http/request.go#L523) making both [INLINE_CODE] and [INLINE_CODE] to "", the HTTP Host header will be "". (See https://github.com/golang/go/issues/11206))
5. But when the engine-api is built with Go<=1.4, Go [won't clean up the Host](https://github.com/golang/go/

query_title: Whether or not to use systemd on host to babysit rkt process
query_body:
There are both pros and cons on whether or not to use systemd to babysit the rkt process.

Pros of using host systemd:
- The process are grouped into the cgroup slice created by systemd, makes it easier to clean up remaining process when the pod's crash. e.g. https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2384
- More reliable way to get the [INLINE_CODE] timestamp (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23887) of the whole pod, e.g. we can add a hook to write down the timestamp in [INLINE_CODE] when a pod exits.

Cons:
- Not easy to implement [INLINE_CODE] [feature](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23335#issuecomment-204180056) when running as a systemd service. ([INLINE_CODE] has the [INLINE_CODE] options. but [INLINE_CODE] doesn't cc @albal @iaguis 
- Race between cgroups is created and detected by cAdvisor, and the pod is actually running. When run as a systemd service, the systemd creates the cgroup for rkt, this can happen before the pod is running, so cAdvisor will see the cgroup and query the rkt api service for the pods, but the api service will return the pod is not running. See here for a [clearer explanation.](https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2341#issuecomment-203455155)

I think both pros and cons can be solved in one way or another. 
If we don't use systemd on host:
- We can implement the [INLINE_CODE] in rkt, but ignore the situation when it's impossible to write down anything (e.g. stage1 or PID1 is killed)

If we use systemd on host:
- For the [INLINE_CODE], can we have systemd to support [INLINE_CODE] for [INLINE_CODE]?
- For the cAdvisor issue, there are several ideas:
 - Just ignore the pod level cgroup(which is created by systemd before the pod is running), however this is not preferrable as we miss the resource usage of the pod's s

target_title: Kubelet's logic of checking docker running in host does not work in systemd distro
target_body:
I notice that kubelet does not create "/docker-daemon" cgroup if docker is managed by systemd, because the function isProcessRunningInHost call (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L448) returns false. As a result, test cases in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/test/e2e/kubelet_perf.go will all fail. This isProcessRunningInHost function (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go#L408) compares /proc/1/ns/mnt with /proc/<docker pid>/ns/mnt to determine if docker is running in host. But this is not true if docker is managed by systemd (such as in CoreOS). You can see that docker has different mount namespace from pid 1, if docker is managed by systemd. But docker and pid 1 process have the same pid namespace.

Why would kubelet check the mount namespace, instead of pid namespace? Could you fix this issue in kubelet container manager?

@dchen1107 @vishh

query_title: Support Cassandra in PetSet
query_body:
**I haven't deployed Cassandra to production, I'll incorporate comments from anyone who has into this missive.**

A cassandra cluster is a ring of nodes. 
- Clients send request to any node (coordinator) which forwards requests to the node with the data.
- Each node is assigned a token. Each row is hashed based on a partition function applied on its primary key. A node stores hashes between its token and the next node's token. 
- A replication strategy picks how data is replicated, eg: 'SimpleStrategy' picks the next N nodes in the ring. The coordinator is also responsible for proxying writes to these nodes based on the consistency level of the request.
## Initial Deployment

To deploy a cassandra cluster you need to pick some "seed" nodes. These are nodes that come up first, and that all other nodes contact to get information about the cluster. They're only used in bootstrapping, after which all nodes cache their peers. All nodes in a cluster must have the same seed. Without at least one seed node, no nodes can join the cluster.

There appear to be many common ways to pick a seed:
See http://docs.datastax.com/en/archived/cassandra/1.0/docs/cluster_architecture/gossip.html.
- Priam uses Amazon's simpleDB to store each node's id as it comes up, and allocates the first in each DC as a seed (https://github.com/Netflix/Priam/wiki/Setup#s3-bucket-and-simpledb-domains). This requires centralized storage that isn't attached to any pet.
- Our [example](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/tree/master/examples/cassandra) uses Service resolution thorugh a custom entrypoint. If a node finds no endpoints in the Service, it inserts it's own IP into the seed list (TODO: follow up, this feels racy).

Perils:
- Setting all nodes as seeds
- Setting different seeds for different node

query_title: Add transient archive volume type that stores arbitrarily complex file structure
query_body:
Used for cases where pre-initialized data of arbitrary type can be provided to a pod. Similar use case to ([#13610](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13610)) however expanded to support arbitrarily complex structures.
1. Archive Format support for tar, zip or other archive format (preferably with compression/encryption).
2. Extracted to host or memdisk prior to container execution and and linked similar to emptyDir.
3. Contents while Mutable are lost upon pod termination.
4. Archive location could be from local file, http, or other compatible endpoint.

Use Cases:
1. Providing larger configuration/reference files of any format such as SQLite configuration databases.
2. Providing complex pre-configured file structures such as static websites with images.

This would likely require ([#13606](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13606))
target_title: Add an inline volume type that stores small amounts of RO data with the manifest
target_body:
For cases where a small amount of static data is desired. This could include
1. configuration for containers whose process is configured by files
2. small-medium amounts of static data, such as an archive of www data for a static site server
3. inputs to a process that has a small input to work ratio

Example use cases:
- allow developers to specify data along side the pod it's used with, instead of needing to put it "somewhere else" (EBS / PD / RBD)
- allow Kubernetes-native process coordinators to pass input data to worker pods

For developers, this would be facilitated by a kubectl plugin (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/13606) in a similar way to what is proposed for easing secret creation (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/4822). The plugin would handle archive creation and encoding for inclusion in the manifest.

The size of this data would be limited, as it would be living in etcd. I don't know what a reasonable limit is as I'm not familiar enough with etcd. I would assume a couple hundred KB at the most?

target_title: Kubelet: Switch to Docker engine-api and add timeout for all docker calls
target_body:
From the first release of Kubernetes, we have been using [go-dockerclient](https://github.com/fsouza/go-dockerclient). It is reliable and updated frequently. However, we still met some problems when using it:
- **No operation timeout.** Functions in go-dockerclient don’t have timeout. Once the Docker daemon hangs, these caller will also hang forever. (Related issues: #9896, #13934, #21029, #21821, #22259 etc.)
- **No compatibility guarantee.** It's not official Docker client. After each Docker release, community people gradually find and fix compatible issues. (Related issue: #19720 etc.).
- **Missing features.** Some wanted features are not supported by go-dockerclient yet. (Related issue: image pull progress #19077 etc.)

Docker [engine-api](https://github.com/docker/engine-api) is the official Golang client for the Docker remote api. It has **cancellable operations**(All the functions use [Context](https://golang.org/x/net/context)), **official support**(The Docker CLI itself is relying on it) and **the same feature set with Docker CLI**. So, we decided to switch to docker engine-api.

[[INLINE_CODE]](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/dockertools/docker.go#L58) is an abstract interface containing a subset functions of go-dockerclient. Kubelet uses it whenever talking to docker. To switch to engine-api, we must refactor all the functions in [INLINE_CODE] which will touch a lot of code.
To avoid a huge refactoring in one PR, we'll split the refactoring into several steps:
- [x] Implement the original [INLINE_CODE] with the engine-api. [#23506]
- [x] Refactor the functions in the DockerInterface one by one, and add unit test for complex functions [#24748]:
 - [x] ListContainers [#23699]
 - [x] InspectContainer [#23699]
 - [x] CreateContain

query_title: Eliminate the docker load from the production
query_body:
We built docker images for master components for dev cluster on the fly (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/5011) before 1.0 release, which uses docker load instead of docker pull from the registry. The initial proposal I made is targeting for dev and test cluster since there is no proper release tag associated with it. Unfortunately, later we abused this functionality to the most master components except etcd image. In 1.2 release, we even abused this more to load kube-proxy image on each node. 

This is bad because
- There is no uniform way to get system images. For example, on master node, etcd image is pulled from gcr.io, while rest of images are loaded through script; on worker node, fluentd image is pulled from gcr.io, while kube-proxy image is loaded through script.
- Docker load sometimes hung. To self-healing, I introduced a simple logic to timeout that procedure and restart docker daemon as a workaround. That is a hacky way which makes the node bootstrap even more complicated. 
- gcr.io collects many useful stats, and we cannot use them. 

The initial counter argument to do docker load is that people feel gcs is more reliable than gcr. But that is not true today, not even mentioning that some of critical images are pulled from gcr at the first place.

cc/ @mikedanese @roberthbailey
target_title: Design: Build docker images for master components for dev cluster on the fly
target_body:
@ArtfulCoder has pending PR to run etcd_server in a pod, which is pretty much ready to go any minutes. 

Now we want to have other master components running inside a pod / pods. For GKE, this should be easy since it only upgrades to a proper release, from which we could build docker image and push to some repository. But there are the issues for dev cluster. @ArtfulCoder and I discussed this, and now we have two proposals on the table, and both have pros and cons:

**Idea 1:** Build docker images for each release build and tag it with kubernete-dev version bit, and push those images tar file through salt:

pros: 
- The same building process could be re-used for GKE and other cloud provider for production release.
- We can use salt to push docker image directly to master node without complicated feature supported in kubelet.

cons: 
- Everytime when we build a development release, we have to update manifest file for those mater component with new image tag from version bit. 
- More dependency on salt which we want to get rid of

**Idea 2:** Build docker images on master node at runtime. Kubelet is watching a managed directory, and get inotify on changes. When new binary is pushed to master node, kubelet is notified, and create image from scratch, and tell docker to reload newly created image, then restart containers.

pros:
- No update to manifest file for master components for each build

cons:
- It is pretty complicated when I were typing the idea. 
- It requires some special code in kubelet and other components. 

Any more ideas? or suggestions? or objections?

target_title: Containers startup throttling
target_body: # Throttling study ## Summary The purpose of Kubernetes is to orchestrate many, potentially big, applications that could be co-located on shared minions. Kubernetes’ current policy when starting PODs is to start them asap. This can be sub-optimal for OLTP applications where many processes/threads are started. During normal operation, those processes/threads are mostly idling, waiting for the next transaction, but when they are starting, they are CPU and IO greedy. Starting all those processes simultaneously can cause start-up time degradation due to context switching and I/O saturation. In that case, starting them in a controlled manner can improve the start-up time and its predictability. This study proposes to implement a throttling mechanism to improve start-up time predictability. It covers different possible policies, their pros/cons and implications. ## Table of Contents - [Throttling study](#throttling-study) - [Summary](#summary) - [Problematic](#problematic) - [Running does not imply Ready](#running-does-not-imply-ready) - [Need for throttling](#need-for-throttling) - [1. concurrency between the starting POD and the ready ones which are running on the same machine](#1-concurrency-between-the-starting-pod-and-the-ready-ones-which-are-running-on-the-same-machine) - [2. concurrency between the starting containers and the other starting ones of the same POD](#2-concurrency-between-the-starting-containers-and-the-other-starting-ones-of-the-same-pod) - [Protect the ready PODs from the starting ones on the same machine](#protect-the-ready-pods-from-the-starting-ones-on-the-same-machine) - [Limit the number of processes that are starting at a given time](#limit-the-number-of-proce

query_title: Informer should not saturate workqueue with sync events
query_body:
Initial discussion is in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/24323
#### Problem:

When cluster is large and a periodic relist happens, a large number of RCs added by Sync event will block the work queue, thus RCs added by Added/Updated/Deleted event may have a long latency(those events are usually caused by users, they should be processed ASAP).

> I have done a benchmark about replication_controller: if we have 1000 namespace, each have 10 RCs, each RC have 10 replicas(so, 100, 000 pod in total), when periodic list happens, replication_controller need 20s to process the RCs added into work queue by relist, which means if a user create a new RC just at that time, it will be processed after 20 seconds. Users are always captious and impatient.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23394 propose to distinguish relist and resync, but that's not enough:

> IIUC, use replication_controller as example:
> - Relist means "reflector send LIST request to etcd, replace local cache with items get form etcd, and put all deltas to a queue, then the controller framework pop deltas from the queue and put the RC need to process to work queue".
> - Resync means "go through the items in the local cache, put all RCs(in local cache) to work queue".
> 
> Since both relist and resync will add ALL RCs(all RCs from etcd when relist, all RCs from local storage when resync) to work queue, when cluster is large, a large number of RCs will block work queue for a long time. If a unfortunate user create a new RC just at that time, he will get a bad user experience.
#### Proposal

If my understanding of relist/resync is correct, I propose to let [work queue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/controller/replication/replication_controller.go#L93) respect priori
target_title: Split the "resync interval" on reflectors into "relist interval" and "resync interval"
target_body:
Today the resync interval on a controller forces a LIST, and then as a consequence sends all objects down the reflector. However, for most controllers LIST is necessary because 
1. Watch is reliable
2. They do not mutate the store themselves and thus might have data out of sync with etcd
3. They do not "drop" events when failures happen (instead they requeue)
4. Their source of data is relatively up to date, or isn't vulnerable to event reordering (B happens before A and is therefore ignored).

We should split "sync" into "sync" (send all events to listeners) and "list" (clear the cache and fetch from etcd).

All reflectors against etcd should have long "list" intervals (12-24h). Controllers that don't mutate the store or drop events should have long relist intervals AND resync intervals. For controllers that drop events or mutate the store in a potentially inconsistent way, we should relist infrequently and resync frequently.

The following reflectors are "fast" - every 30s

[CODE_BLOCK]

These reflectors should have a 24h relist. We should separate resync, then tune each appropriately.

query_title: rkt: Support dynamic pod.
query_body:
Today, rkt's pod is immutable, which means once started, all the changes made to the pod or the containers within the pod will require the pod to be restarted.

As we are moving towards mutable pods in the future, rkt should support container level interfaces, which can also benefit us from making the container runtime interface more generic and runtime agnostic https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/22964 , as well as implement something like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/23567

Ref https://github.com/coreos/rkt/issues/2375
target_title: Revisit Container Runtime interface
target_body:
In many threads / meetings I mentioned that we are not satisfied with today's container runtime interface due to many reasons. Here are the top reasons off my head:
- Duplicated code for supporting SyncPod for all container runtime implementations, especially with Kubernetes defined policy: StartPolicy, PullPolicy, etc. We talked about changing today's declarative API to imperative API at this lowest extensible point. 
- Tight coupled with image format: docker runtime supports docker image, while rkt support appc image by converting docker image to its own format. In a long run, we want to add support for other image format without changing each runtime. There is no easy way to achieve that goal with today's API.
- Logging management is very different on different os distro and with different runtime implementation. We should make this pluggable with runtime.
- Part of resource isolation is handled by runtime today, while another part is handled by Kubelet. The decision is ad-hoc without much thinking. We need to decide if we want runtime interface to handle resource management or completely hand over to ResourceManager module in Kubelet since qos policy is defined by Kubernetes, and it might be redefined over releases. 
- ...

In my mind, we should separate image management, resource / cgroup management, logging management from today's runtime interface. After this effort, we effectively make today's runtime interface as pod / container lifecycle management interface.

query_title: Is there a way to generate yml files that will produce the existing cluster?
query_body:
Given a kubernetes cluster that is running some number of pods, services, deployments, etc, I would like to generate one or more files ( yml format preferred) that would re-produce the current configuration, when applied to a new cluster.

My use case is a promotion system. I have my 'stack files' as yml files in a git repo, but I need to allow humans to approve changes before they are applied to the cluster.

One way to do this is to use an 'open loop' system. I can use tags or other mechanisms to determine which versions have been applied to the cluster, and then compare the latest version available with the latest deployed version. 

The problem with the open-loop system is that it does not consider that changes could have been made outside the files, or that changes applied could have had problems, etc. 

If I could extract the 'equivalent' files from a running cluster, I could compare them with the ones that are about to be applied. This is a much stronger, 'closed loop' system-- it is able to correctly understand what will happen when the changes are applied, even if we have lost track of the real target state.

if there were such a thing as kubectl apply -f <filename> --dry-run, which lists only the changes that will be made, rather than actually doing the changes, that would work as well. That is already being discussed over at issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/11488

Does anyone have thoughts on this? We are new to kubernetes, but we have created the the functionality I'm describing above for our RedHat/Satellite rpm-based deployments, so i want to re-create it in K8s. Of course, in k8s, we have the complexity that the infrastructure itself can change, not just installed package versions!
target_title: kubectl --dry-run
target_body:
kubectl should support a --dry-run option for every mutation to show what it would do, without actually doing it

We might need API changes in order to make this high-fidelity. For instance, if we wanted to know what a pod config would look like after admission control populated defaults, we'd need to execute most of the creation path.

query_title: Disk based evictions
query_body:
Local disk is shared amongst pods and system daemons on a best effort today. Since we do not support disk as a first class resource, there is no means to restrict disk usage of pods.
Often times, nodes run out of local disk, and kubelet needs to free up disk space. Kubelet can perform several actions to free up disk space - delete old containers, delete unused images, evict pods that use a lot of disk. 
This issue tracks the overall effort of freeing up disk space on demand by the Kubelet.
- [x] Proposal for disk eviction PR - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/25237
- [x] Introduce disk eviction thresholds
- [x] Add support for pod evictions
- [x] Generate disk pressure condition in Kubelet
- [x] Update Scheduler to not schedule pods whenever disk pressure condition is set on a node
- [ ] Refactor image GC such that they it can be run on demand based on eviction thresholds
- [ ] Update Container GC to keep the minimum number of containers that kubelet needs (2 for now) and delete the rest of them by default immediately.
- [ ] e2e tests

---

**Stretch**
- [ ] Extract logs outside of containers and delete containers immediately - depends on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/24702
- [ ] Delete logs and images based on thresholds
target_title: Serialize and write api.Pod/Container spec/status as container annotations
target_body:
Forked from the discussion in #23725.

In short, we've been writing information as docker labels and rkt annotations to container/pods due to the lack of kubelet checkpointing. As the results, we have to handle label/annotation backward compatibility issues. Instead of doing that, we can just serialize the kubernetes pod/container objects and write it as annotations.

After discussing with @vishh and @dchen1107, we may also checkpoint the pod "status" (instead of just the spec), so that we can delete an container as soon as the new one starts.

There are two options:
1. Write the entire pod object (spec/status) to every container in the pod. This is easy to implement, and the last created container has the complete spec and status. 
2. Write pod spec/status to the pod sandbox (i.e., infra container for docker), and container spec/status to individual containers. This is cleaner in general.

@Random-Liu, feel free to grab this one since you were working on docker labels. 
@dchen1107, I marked this v1.3 tentatively.

/cc @kubernetes/sig-node

query_body:
## Problem

Our code is riddled with snippets that look like this:

[CODE_BLOCK]

These lines bubble errors up the call stack until someone decides to log them and move on:

[CODE_BLOCK]

Which can yield an unhelpful error message like (fake, but not totally unreasonable):

[CODE_BLOCK]

And now we're tasked with trying to crawl through the code to figure out where that error actually came from.

We discourage logging an error that's also returned (duplicate log statements interwoven throughout the code can also be confusing), but if you (the person debugging) is lucky someone has attached a unique context message that can help you find the source (e.g. [INLINE_CODE]).
## Assumptions
- Errors are relatively uncommon - i.e. this doesn't apply to "not found" errors that should probably be [INLINE_CODE]s, or errors which can be generated in a tight loop
- Errors are ephemeral - that is, they are handled (e.g. logged) and then discarded (not stored anywhere)
- When an error is produced, it is not always possible to know how it will be handled, or even how severe it is
## Proposal

From the above assumptions, I get 2 guiding principles:
1. If returning an error, it is your job to provide the maximum amount of debugging information and context around that error.
2. If handling an error, it is your job to use the _appropriate_ context for the specific case (e.g. a critical failure should have more detail than something that is expected to occassionally fail and will be retried).

To this end, I'd like to create a kubernetes error package that we promote everywhere. The constructor could look something like (rough sketch, not final API):

target_title: There should be a single way that pods and other resources are identified in k8s component logs wherever possible
target_body:
Currently there is no single way that pods are identified in log messages, which can make it difficult to find all the messages relevant to a single pod in a log file. I think, wherever possible, that we should identify pods with the following information, formatted consistently:
1. Pod name
2. Pod namespace
3. Pod UID

It's possible that not all call sites will have all of this information; in that case, we should stick to the format, and just log empty fields. I started thinking about this in the context of the kubelet but it applies to anything that logs messages identifying pods.

query_title: Speed up getting pod statuses in PLEG when there are many changes
query_body:
Forked from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/23591#issuecomment-203042820
Creating a new issue so I won't forget.

PLEG serially gets status for every pod, where at least one container has encountered a state transition. This becomes the bottleneck if a lot of containers changed in one relist period. We were aware of this problem and had come up with a few options before:
1. Add a new GetPodStatus variant to bypass the [INLINE_CODE] call since pleg already have this information. The downside is that this is a very docker-specific optimization and doesn't make sense for other runtimes.
2. Parallelize the process.
3. Do nothing. Assume docker is busy and process slowly.

I think we can do (2) with a small number of goroutines (e.g., 2) to speed up the time.

target_title: Eliminate the need for namespaces with URI names
target_body:
Kubernetes has done a nice job simplifying cluster configuration and eliminating sources of conflict across separately developed services. Kubernetes namespaces are an attempt to apply this approach to naming within a cluster. Unfortunately, in this case, the result is to confuse rather than simplify cluster naming.
A good example of the confusion caused by namespaces is resource type naming. In the ‘Kubernetes-defined resource types’ section the predefined resource namespace is specified as resources.kubernetes.io. The predefined resource type names are all of the form kubernetes.io/resources/<resource-name>. The redundancy of these shows the problem with this design. It is a microcosm of the problem that would exist if the web had used this design instead of URIs. 
IMHO, Kubernetes would be well-served by ditching its namespace-based naming design and replacing it with names that are URIs.

query_title: Kubernetes Master High Availability Proposal
query_body: # High Availability Kubernetes Clusters Promotion ## Introduction There have been attempts in achieving high-availability master in the community: - [High Availability: kubelet doesn't try to talk to a different API server in case of failures](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/18174) - [allow the restclient to contact multiple apiservers](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/25428) But the feature of multiple apiserver isn't going to make it into v1.3. **Moreover, the method of a load balancer in front of the multiple apiservers is still very popular for high-availability master deployment**. So in this document we present a proposal on how to setup high-availability master using haproxy as the loadbalancer, especailly in private cloud scenarios. It enriches the previous document ([http://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/high-availability/](http://kubernetes.io/docs/admin/high-availability/)) with more details in the following two aspects: 1. **All components except kubelet are dockerized**. query_title: Proposal: informer redesign
query_body:
(To continue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/27004#issuecomment-225643876)

Recently, we have found a race in informer in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/27004. Although the P0 issue has been fixed as quickly as possible, we agreed that we should redesign it properly after 1.3 release: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/27004#issuecomment-225969446, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/27341#discussion_r67003455, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/27341#issuecomment-225921010.

The problem of current informer design is that it couples queue and store. This has caused some races. Wojtek has done a great job fixing it for 1.3 release. I am reluctantly pointing out that it's not the ideal solution. First, it couples the queue and store with complicated locking; Second, it's really hard to maintain if someone wants to change the code in the future.
![f3f57e10-314b-11e6-9814-32c555988dc6](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/920884/16105411/0f38225a-333f-11e6-8e3e-4c9f964da6a1.png)

One redesign choice we made is serialize all updates on store inside controller:
![b3741b74-3170-11e6-8020-eadab862ba10](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/920884/16101359/ba072ce2-3319-11e6-917a-6a48e94cc3bf.png)
Now the queue wouldn't talk to store anymore. The diff comparison on Relisting, iterating items in Resync will be serialized along with Add/Update/Delete operations inside controller. Controller is the only one that mades changes upon store.
With this redesign, we should be more confident to guarantee race-free in informer, and separate concerns of sub-components. This will improve maintainability and ease mindset of future maintainer, contributor.

Finally, I want to give a big shoutout for Wojtek for the qu
target_title: Race condition in Informer
target_body:
### What's the issue?

Informer could end up in wrong state.
### Example?

I have been stress testing RC of 100 replicas. I kept deleting the pod and let RC recover it to 100. The program will do informer.store.List() to check if there are 100 pods. But at the end of day it returned more than 100 (e.g. 131), while listing directly from apiserver returned 100.
### Why?

Informer has a queue and a store (aka indexer) internally.
- The store relies on the queue to do blocking [pop()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/controller/framework/controller.go#L127-L128) and and then [updates itself](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/controller/framework/shared_informer.go#L200-L224) in [Process()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/controller/framework/controller.go#L127-L128).
- The queue (delta fifo) is used to queue events from watcher. For [each operation in reflector](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/client/cache/reflector.go#L384-L392), e.g. Delete, we will [enqueue an event to the queue](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/client/cache/delta_fifo.go#L200).
- However, in DeltaFIFO.Delete(), it will [check the store](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0d3be6a316b39a71b62d45272d339f7fa9162165/pkg/client/cache/delta_fifo.go#L192-L198) first to see if it needs to send a delete event. **This logic is wrong because the queue and store are run concurrently. There could be an ADD event not processed by store yet thus queue won't enqueue DELETE event.**
